analysis.title: Macro & Strategy Focus: US productivity: a structural shift is underway
key_insights: US labour productivity (output per hour) has grown at an annualised 2.4% since the post-pandemic recovery and 2.7% since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022. The pre-pandemic decade averaged 1.6%.

The report names three main drivers of the recent gains. They are pandemic-driven digitalisation and reorganisation of production, more intensive use of labour and capital, and the AI infrastructure investment boom.

The payoff from actually using AI (efficiency gains) does not yet clearly show up in aggregate data. Industry-level data and firm surveys suggest the fastest AI adopters have enjoyed the fastest gains.

The authors conclude the US has likely entered a high labour productivity growth regime. Productivity growth should stay structurally higher than before the pandemic even as the impetus from AI capital spending fades.

The framework splits labour productivity into capital deepening, labour quality, TFP (total factor productivity) and factor utilisation. Only TFP reflects true innovation and is tied to durable long-run growth, because capital accumulation faces diminishing returns.

TFP is a residual that cannot be measured directly. If GDP is underestimated, so is TFP, and TFP also absorbs anything unmeasured, such as harder work and higher machine utilisation. The San Francisco Fed's utilisation-adjusted TFP series is used as the purer gauge.

Capital deepening has contributed roughly as much to labour productivity over the past four years as in the late-1990s ICT (information and communication technology) boom. AI capex has surged much as IT and communications equipment spending did around 2000.

Factor utilisation turned positive at the end of 2024 and now accounts for more than half of annual labour productivity growth in the latest quarter. This coincided with elevated 2025 policy uncertainty and very little hiring. The recent pick-up in employment suggests this source may be exhausted.

TFP growth rose from 0.8% a year before the pandemic to 1% since, and 1.2% since the end of 2022. It expanded rapidly between late 2022 and 2023 and then barely grew over the past three years. The authors say this is hard to attribute to AI, since adoption kept rising.
The authors attribute the 2022-2023 TFP gain more to pandemic-era digitisation and production reorganisation, helped by earlier cloud infrastructure, than to AI efficiency gains.

Chicago Fed data on 87 industries show the main contributors to aggregate productivity since 2020 are housing, data processing and internet publishing, computer-systems design, online and other retail, and miscellaneous professional services. Gains are concentrated in a handful of industries.

Industries with higher AI adoption show stronger productivity growth versus their 2015-2019 trend, with a J-curve pattern in which productivity dips as firms invest before rising. Part of this may be capital deepening rather than TFP, likely true of information (home to hyperscalers) but less so of real estate and finance.

An Atlanta Fed survey of 750 executives found AI-related revenue labour productivity gains averaged 0.6% in 2025, with wide dispersion and the largest effects in high-skill services and finance. 16% of that growth came from capital deepening and the rest from TFP. A St Louis Fed study finds a positive link between excess productivity growth and time saved with AI.

The current episode resembles the mid-1990s. Labour productivity has grown faster than in the early ICT years, while TFP lags. During the ICT boom TFP entered its high-growth regime a few quarters after labour productivity did.

The regime-switching model puts labour productivity in a high-growth regime since 2023Q2, while TFP has not yet shifted. The late-1990s regime, from roughly end-1996 to early 2005, shows up clearly for both series. Smoothed probabilities carry hindsight bias in recent periods.
Cyclical forces and slower AI capital spending will probably weigh on factor utilisation and capital intensity through 2028. Wider AI diffusion should lift TFP over time.

Policy implication: AI productivity gains could sustain strong growth without the same degree of inflation pressure. The aggregate AI effect on the labour market has been limited so far, but that may change depending on whether AI complements or replaces workers.

macro_indicators.indicator: US labour productivity growth (output per hour), annualised
macro_indicators.reading: 2.4% since the post-pandemic recovery, 2.7% since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, versus a 1.6% average in the decade before the pandemic
macro_indicators.interpretation: Productivity growth is running well above the pre-pandemic trend. The authors read this as a shift to a high-growth regime, which supports growth without matching inflation pressure.
macro_indicators.period: post-pandemic recovery to date, since Nov 2022

macro_indicators.indicator: US TFP growth (San Francisco Fed, utilisation-adjusted), annualised
macro_indicators.reading: 0.8% before the pandemic, 1% since, 1.2% since the end of 2022
macro_indicators.interpretation: Only tentative acceleration. TFP barely grew over the past three years, so AI efficiency gains are not yet visible in aggregate data.

macro_indicators.reading: High-growth regime since 2023Q2 for labour productivity, TFP not yet shifted
macro_indicators.interpretation: The model result is the authors' estimate, not an official figure, and recent-period regime calls carry more uncertainty. The pattern mirrors the late 1990s, when TFP lagged labour productivity by several quarters.

macro_indicators.indicator: Factor utilisation contribution to labour productivity growth
macro_indicators.reading: More than half of annual labour productivity growth in the latest quarter
macro_indicators.interpretation: Firms squeezed more from existing staff amid little hiring. The authors say this source has limited room left and the recent employment pick-up suggests the limit may be reached.

macro_indicators.indicator: Capital intensity and factor utilisation contributions to productivity
macro_indicators.reading: Expected to weigh on productivity growth through 2028
macro_indicators.interpretation: Cyclical forces and slower AI capital spending are expected to reduce these contributions, with TFP from wider AI diffusion taking over over time.

risk_factors: Factor utilisation gains may already be exhausted, as the recent employment pick-up suggests.
Slower AI capital spending and cyclical forces could weigh on capital intensity and utilisation through 2028.
TFP is a residual, so GDP mismeasurement or unmeasured effort and utilisation can distort the read on AI's contribution, and the data are often revised during structural change.
AI productivity gains are concentrated in a subset of firms and sectors, so aggregate gains may be slow to appear.
Regime-switching estimates for recent periods are less certain, and smoothed probabilities carry hindsight bias.
The labour market effect of AI could grow, depending on whether AI complements or replaces workers.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 decomposes annual US labour productivity growth into capital intensity, labour quality, TFP and factor utilisation. TFP gains remain modest compared with the late-1990s tech boom.

Exhibit 5 plots AI usage as a percentage of businesses in June 2026 against annualised productivity growth (output per worker) from 2022Q4 to 2026Q2 relative to the 2015-2019 trend, by industry. Industries with greater AI adoption show stronger gains, with information at the top right.
Exhibits 6 and 7 compare the current episode with the early 1990s. Labour productivity is rising faster than then, while TFP is lagging somewhat.

tension_points.bull_case: Industries and firms that use AI most show faster labour productivity growth. The Atlanta Fed survey found a 0.6% average gain in 2025, and the mid-1990s ICT precedent suggests TFP follows labour productivity by a few quarters, so aggregate gains should become visible.
tension_points.bear_case: TFP expanded rapidly between late 2022 and 2023 and then barely grew over the past three years, which is hard to attribute to AI. Sector gains may reflect capital deepening, and the gains are concentrated in a few industries, so the aggregate data do not yet show an AI effect.

theme_stances.key_argument: Labour productivity growth should stay structurally higher than before the pandemic even as AI capital spending fades, because AI gains are nascent and set to widen.
theme_stances.evidence: the US has likely entered a high labour productivity growth regime

theme_stances.key_argument: AI efficiency gains do not yet clearly show up in aggregate TFP, which barely grew over the past three years, though industry-level gains are visible.
theme_stances.evidence: barely grew over the past three years
